prompt: What forms when a terminal alkyne, RC≡CH, is treated with sodium amide, NaNH2?

choices.text: The acetylide anion RC≡C^− (as its Na+ salt) and NH3

choices.why: Amide ion acts as a base here: it removes the terminal hydrogen as H^+ and becomes NH3.
Nothing adds to the triple bond. The base removes the terminal hydrogen and the triple bond stays intact.

choices.text: Nothing; hydrocarbons are too weakly acidic to react
choices.why: Terminal alkynes are relatively acidic (acetylene's pK_a is 25), so a strong base like NaNH2 removes the terminal hydrogen.

explanation: Terminal alkynes are relatively acidic, the most striking difference between alkenes and alkynes. Sodium amide removes the terminal hydrogen to give the corresponding acetylide anion, with ammonia as the by-product.

prompt: According to the Brønsted–Lowry definition, which compounds can act as acids?

choices.text: Any compound containing a hydrogen atom, under the right circumstances
Only oxyacids, such as H2SO4 and HNO3, that contain O–H bonds
choices.why: These are the acids we usually think of, but any hydrogen-containing compound can donate H^+ under the right circumstances.

choices.text: Only halogen acids, such as HCl and HBr, in aqueous solution
choices.why: These are familiar acids, but hydrocarbons such as acetylene can also donate H^+.

choices.text: Only compounds whose acidic hydrogen is bonded to oxygen or a halogen
choices.why: Hydrocarbons can be acids too: acetylene has pK_a = 25.

explanation: A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a substance that donates H^+. Although we usually think of oxyacids (H2SO4, HNO3) or halogen acids (HCl, HBr), any compound containing a hydrogen atom can be an acid under the right circumstances, hydrocarbons included.

prompt: What is the pK_a of acetylene?
explanation: Table 9.7.1 gives acetylene a pK_a of 25 (K_a = 10^−25). That makes it far more acidic than ethylene (pK_a = 44) or methane (pK_a ≈ 60).

prompt: Which list ranks these hydrocarbons from most acidic to least acidic?

choices.why: That is reversed. A lower pK_a means a stronger acid: acetylene (25), then ethylene (44), then methane (about 60).
Acetylene, pK_a 25, is more acidic than ethylene, pK_a 44.
Methane (pK_a about 60) is the weakest acid of the three. Ethylene's pK_a is 44.

explanation: A lower pK_a corresponds to a stronger acid. Acetylene (pK_a = 25) is the most acidic, then ethylene (pK_a = 44), then methane (pK_a ≈ 60). This follows the s character of the orbital holding the anion's charge: sp > sp2 > sp3.

prompt: Table 9.7.1 gives K_a = 10^−25 for acetylene and K_a = 10^−44 for ethylene. Acetylene's K_a is larger by a factor of 10 raised to what power?
explanation: 10^−25 ÷ 10^−44 = 10^19. Acetylene's K_a is 10^19 times larger than ethylene's, matching the difference in their pK_a values, 44 − 25 = 19.

prompt: Acetylene (pK_a = 25) can be deprotonated by the conjugate base of which acids?

choices.text: Any acid whose pK_a is greater than 25
Any acid whose pK_a is less than 25
choices.why: The conjugate base of a stronger acid (lower pK_a) is a weaker base. The base has to come from a weaker acid than acetylene, with pK_a above 25.

choices.text: Any acid whose pK_a is less than 16
choices.why: These conjugate bases are too weak. Hydroxide, for example, comes from water (pK_a 15.7). The acid's pK_a must be greater than 25.
Oxyacids are strong acids with weak conjugate bases. The base must come from an acid with pK_a above 25.

explanation: Acetylene, pK_a = 25, can be deprotonated by the conjugate base of any acid whose pK_a is greater than 25. Amide ion (NH2^−), the conjugate base of ammonia (pK_a = 35), is often used to deprotonate terminal alkynes.

prompt: Which base is strong enough to deprotonate acetylene (pK_a = 25)?

choices.why: Water (15.7) is a stronger acid than acetylene (25), so hydroxide is too weak a base.
Methanol (15.6) is a stronger acid than acetylene (25), so methoxide is too weak a base.
Carbonic acid (6.4) is a far stronger acid than acetylene, so bicarbonate is much too weak a base.

explanation: A base can remove H^+ from acetylene if its conjugate acid has a pK_a greater than 25. Ammonia's pK_a is 35, so amide ion (NH2^−) deprotonates acetylene, and it is often used for terminal alkynes.

prompt: What is the pK_a of ammonia, the conjugate acid of the amide ion used to deprotonate terminal alkynes?
explanation: Ammonia's pK_a is 35. Because 35 is greater than acetylene's 25, amide ion (NH2^−) is a strong enough base to deprotonate terminal alkynes.

prompt: What percent s character does the orbital holding the negative charge of an acetylide anion have?
explanation: The acetylide carbon is sp-hybridized, so its negative charge sits in an orbital with 50% s character, compared with 33% for a vinylic (sp2) anion and 25% for an alkyl (sp3) anion.

prompt: To the nearest whole percent, what percent s character does the orbital holding the negative charge of a vinylic anion have?
explanation: A vinylic anion has an sp2-hybridized carbon, so the charge sits in an orbital with 33% s character. That falls between the acetylide anion (sp, 50%) and the alkyl anion (sp3, 25%).

prompt: Why does more s character stabilize the negative charge of a carbon anion?

choices.text: s orbitals are nearer the positive nucleus and lower in energy than p orbitals
s orbitals are larger and farther from the nucleus than p orbitals
choices.why: It is the reverse: s orbitals are nearer the nucleus, and holding the charge close to the nucleus stabilizes it.

choices.text: More s character lets the orbital hold more electrons
choices.why: Each orbital holds the same lone pair. What changes is how close to the nucleus the charge is held.

choices.text: More s character makes the carbon positively charged
choices.why: The carbon still carries the negative charge. It is simply held closer to the nucleus and so stabilized.

explanation: Because s orbitals are nearer the positive nucleus and lower in energy than p orbitals, a negative charge is stabilized more in an orbital with higher s character. So acetylide anions (50% s) are more stable than vinylic (33%) or alkyl (25%) anions, and terminal alkynes are more acidic than alkenes or alkanes.

prompt: According to the section, how does holding an anion's negative charge closer to the carbon nucleus change the way that carbon looks in an electrostatic potential map?

choices.text: The carbon appears less negative (less red)
The carbon appears more negative (more red)
choices.why: Figure 9.7.1 shows the reverse: placing the charge closer to the nucleus makes the carbon appear less negative.
The carbon still carries a negative charge. It just looks less negative.

choices.text: The map looks the same, since every anion carries a −1 charge
choices.why: The charges are equal, but the maps differ: the acetylide carbon, whose charge is held closest to the nucleus, looks least negative.

explanation: Figure 9.7.1 compares alkyl, vinylic and acetylide anions. Its electrostatic potential maps show that placing the negative charge closer to the carbon nucleus, as in the sp-hybridized acetylide anion, makes the carbon appear less negative (red).

prompt: The pK_a of acetone, CH3COCH3, is 19.3. Which base is strong enough to deprotonate acetone?

choices.why: Water (15.7) is a stronger acid than acetone (19.3), so hydroxide is not a strong enough base.
Methanol (15.6) is a stronger acid than acetone (19.3), so methoxide is not a strong enough base.
Carbonic acid (6.4) is a far stronger acid than acetone, so bicarbonate is much too weak a base.

explanation: A base can deprotonate acetone if its conjugate acid is a weaker acid than acetone, with a pK_a greater than 19.3. Only acetylene (pK_a = 25) qualifies, so sodium acetylide works and the other three bases don't (Exercise 9.7.1).

prompt: Sodium acetylide, HC≡C^− Na+, is mixed with each of the following. Which one can it NOT deprotonate?

choices.why: Water is a stronger acid than acetylene (pK_a 25), so acetylide removes its proton.
Methanol is a stronger acid than acetylene, so acetylide removes its proton.
Acetone is a stronger acid than acetylene. Exercise 9.7.1 shows that acetylide deprotonates it.

explanation: Acetylide anion can remove H^+ only from acids stronger than its own conjugate acid, acetylene (pK_a = 25). Water, methanol and acetone all have pK_a values below 25. Ethylene, with pK_a = 44, is a much weaker acid, so acetylide can't deprotonate it.

prompt: Why don't methane and ethylene react with any of the common bases?

choices.text: They have no hydrogen atoms that a base could remove
choices.why: Both have C–H hydrogens, and any compound with a hydrogen can be an acid under the right circumstances. They are just very weak acids.

choices.text: They are stronger acids than acetylene
choices.why: They are far weaker: pK_a about 60 and 44, compared with acetylene's 25.

choices.text: Their anions would have too much s character
choices.why: More s character stabilizes an anion. Alkyl (25%) and vinylic (33%) anions have less s character than acetylide (50%), which is why they are less stable.

explanation: Table 9.7.1: methane (pK_a ≈ 60) and ethylene (pK_a = 44) are very weak acids and do not react with any of the common bases. Acetylene, with pK_a = 25, can be deprotonated by a strong base such as amide ion.
